How to read the level: On many brand charts, the lowest number marks the deepest end of that brand’s scale.
Common direction to discuss: Discuss whether you mean a visually very deep base or a specific brand’s named shade.
What to watch for: Another brand can label a deep shade differently. Check its own swatch and wording rather than transferring this number across.

Approximate depth description: Very dark brown or soft black-brown
How to read the level: This commonly sits one step above the deepest reference level on charts that use a numbered depth scale.
Common direction to discuss: Describe the target as very dark with visible brown only in brighter light, if that is what you mean.
What to watch for: Lighting can make this level read black in one room and brown in another; a photo is not a substitute for the brand chart.

How to read the level: Read it as a depth position, not as a guarantee of warmth, ashiness, or any particular reflection.
Common direction to discuss: Separate the depth request from the tone request: dark brown is the level language; the tonal family is a second choice.
What to watch for: The starting base can make the same named shade show a different visible cast.

How to read the level: Many charts place this in the brown range between dark and medium-looking brown.
Common direction to discuss: Use it to start a conversation about depth, then point to the brand’s own tone letters or shade description.
What to watch for: Do not expect the chart position to describe the finished tone by itself.

How to read the level: Often a middle brown reference on a brand scale that runs from deepest to lightest.
Common direction to discuss: Say whether your goal is to stay around a medium brown depth or move toward it from your present base.
What to watch for: Porosity, previous colour, and the starting depth can all change how much depth is visible after colouring.

How to read the level: This is a transition area on many charts, where brand names may switch from brown language to blonde language.
Common direction to discuss: Use both a written brand shade name and a swatch viewed in person when possible.
What to watch for: Names are especially inconsistent here; do not rely on the word “blonde” or “brown” alone.

How to read the level: Many scales place it on the blonde side of the transition, but the exact label belongs to each brand.
Common direction to discuss: Describe the depth separately from whether you want a warmer, cooler, or more neutral-looking direction.
What to watch for: A phone image can shift this level strongly with exposure and white balance.

How to read the level: Commonly used as a lighter blonde reference on numbered brand charts.
Common direction to discuss: Ask to compare the intended reference with your starting base under ordinary light before deciding on a formula.
What to watch for: Lift, existing colour, texture, and application process affect what becomes visible; a level is not an outcome guarantee.

How to read the level: On many scales this sits near the light end, above light blonde references.
Common direction to discuss: Use the number only with the exact brand chart in front of you, plus a clear description of the visible tone you are comparing.
What to watch for: Highly light-looking images are sensitive to camera exposure, screen brightness, and the underlying base.

How to read the level: Many common ten-level charts use this as the lightest numbered reference; other brand charts can extend, compress, or rename their scales.
Common direction to discuss: Check whether the specific brand uses ten levels at all before repeating this number as a request.
What to watch for: It is not a global ceiling and it does not predict what a process will produce on any individual starting base.
